newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Foreign developers enter Shanghai housing market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Foreign developers enter Shanghai housing market.

text.p: Foreign property developers are cautiously entering the Shanghai housing market and predict an eventual huge demand for quality homes in China's largest city.
But there is a catch -- how do you guarantee profit when there are currently no precedents in China for re-possessing housing if buyers default on mortgage payments?
Pending an answer to the crucial issue of dealing with payment defaults, developers are testing the waters with only one or two projects each.
Among the foreign developers involved in domestic housing projects in Shanghai, Singapore's DBS Land and Hong Kong's Shui On Properties Ltd are among the most aggressive, analysts say.
DBS announced in January that it would build a housing estate on a 14,900 square metre site in Shanghai's Luwan district, located near the central part of the city.
In the most closely-watched project in Shanghai, Shui On is investing $500 million in a project in the eastern Hongkou district to build 1.7 million square metres of housing, providing 20,000 units.
DEVELOPER PLANS LARGEST FOREIGN-INVESTED PROJECT
Analysts say the project will be the largest foreign-invested commercial housing development in Shanghai to date.
"It's really going to crack the nutty problem of mortgages which have caused problems for other projects," said Sam Crispin, senior manager for property agent First Pacific Davies.

Shui On is cooperating with local banks to offer 70 percent mortgages over a 20-year period, compared with the previous limits of 50 percent and 15 years, to sell directly to individuals, Crispin said.
Analysts said uncertainty over enforcement of mortgage rules significantly raises the risk for Shui On.
Shui On declined to comment on how it will handle the problem of mortgage defaults.
"There are regulations (to deal with mortgage defaults) in place, but they are still untested," Crispin said.
SHANGHAI INCOMES LOW FOR MANY PROSPECTIVE BUYERS
Current income levels in Shanghai are also still too low to allow most ordinary people to aspire to owning their own home bought on the commercial market.

Sale prices for housing on Shanghai's outskirts now range from 2,000 to 3,000 yuan ($241 to $361) per square metre, or around 250,000-300,000 yuan ($30,000-36,000) for a normal apartment, developers said.
In comparison, the average annual salary of Chinese employees is now around 6,200 yuan ($750), according to official figures.
"The demand is definitely there, but the difficulty is where the money is coming from," said one foreign developer. "The little people just don't have the money to acquire property."

Despite these problems, the local city government is trying to persuade foreign real estate firms to help them re-develop Shanghai's dilapidated and inadequate local housing by guaranteeing a 15 percent return on investment in some projects.

Shanghai did little in the way of redevelopment between the communist takeover in 1949 and the early 1990s. The city now wants to relocate people and construct office buildings in central districts, while residents want to upgrade their housing.
DEVELOPERS MUST NEGOTIATE RETURNS
But developers warned the 15 percent return must be negotiated on a case-by-case basis.

"The return depends on which developer, the area of the development and the local officials that the developer is dealing with," said Boris Ying, general manager of China projects for Hong Kong's Ryoden Property Development Co Ltd.
"It's not really an across-the-board thing," he said.
Developers in the Shanghai market are still putting more emphasis on quality office buildings and foreigner housing, where returns for good projects can be as high as 30 to 50 percent, analysts said.
But the local housing market is also one that long term they cannot ignore.
"We do think the ultimate demand for housing will come from the local people," said Peter Kok, director of development and marketing for Hong Kong's Hutchison Whampoa Ltd.
